correctness.rationale: The 16 even-weight five-bit words, adjacent at Hamming distance four, define a 5-regular Clebsch graph. The incidence-count lower bound eliminates four selected vertices: 12 distinct nonempty signatures on 4 chosen positions would require at least 22 outside incidences but 4*5=20. A complete independent first-principles examination of 4368 five-sets found exactly 416 codes in induced types 16 independent, 320 one-edge, 80 four-star. Constructing every one-vertex exchange on all 416 yielded the jump graph 2960 edges, radius5 diameter6, degree types 25/15/9, and the slide graph 1360 edges, radius6 diameter7, degree types 25/7/1; the latter has exactly 80 pendant star states. Every vertex BFS was evaluated, so this is a complete finite proof, not a sample; the actual two verifier source implementations were also inspected and both Git blob identities and full record tree were checked.

originality.rationale: PASS best-of-knowledge. The same finite Clebsch graph is known in generic locating-domination bounds, identifying-code classifications and dominating-set enumeration, but those predicates differ: 96 optimal identifying codes identify all closed neighborhoods, and 1056 five-set dominators impose no external uniqueness; neither determines the 416 open-neighborhood locating-dominating optima or their two reconfiguration graph metrics. The full-text generic 2013 and 2015 locating-domination papers concern global-complement conditions and twin-free bounds, not this full exchange classification. Resultary search found the precise current theorem but no earlier equal/stronger statement. Residual risk of obscure enumerations remains.
residual_risks: A specialised earlier Clebsch location-domination or optimal-code reconfiguration table not indexed by available searches could reduce originality.
The result is an exact finite host classification, not a theorem for all strongly regular graphs.
